who: Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant of Assisi, in Italy. About 1206 he gave everything away, to his father's fury, and lived as a beggar for Christ. The brothers who joined him became the Friars Minor. He preached to birds and to a sultan, kept Christmas with a real manger, and bore wounds like Christ's.

tidbits.text: Preaching before Pope Honorius III and his cardinals, he was so full of joy that “he moved his feet as if dancing”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 73

tidbits.text: He meant to ask the emperor for a law: on Christmas Day everyone should scatter grain on the roads for the birds, “especially our sisters the larks”.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 200

tidbits.text: One year Christmas fell on a Friday, a day without meat, and a brother said so. Francis wished “that the very walls should eat flesh on such a day”.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 199

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In 1181 or 1182, at **Assisi** in Umbria, Italy. His father, **Pietro di Bernardone**, was a rich cloth merchant. His mother was **Pica**.

facts.label: Named
facts.text: Baptised **Giovanni**, or John. His father was in France when he was born, and on his return he renamed the boy **Francesco**.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: On the evening of **3 October 1226**, at the Portiuncula below Assisi. Celano dates it to the Sunday, 4 October.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At San Giorgio in Assisi. In 1230 he was moved to the great church built for him, and hidden deep under its altar.

facts.label: Made a saint
facts.text: **16 July 1228**, at Assisi, by Pope Gregory IX, his old friend and protector.

facts.label: Founded
facts.text: The **Friars Minor**, the Lesser Brothers, in 1209. With Clare, the **Poor Ladies**, today's Poor Clares. Then an order of penance for lay people, now called the Third Order.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Two Rules, a Testament, letters, prayers, 28 short Admonitions and the *Canticle of the Sun*, in the Umbrian speech of his day.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: **Italy**, with Catherine of Siena. Also of animals, and since 1979 of all who care for ecology.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A brown or grey habit tied with a knotted cord, the five wounds, and often birds.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him. He is not on the Orthodox calendar.

facts.label: Pronounced
facts.text: **FRAN-sis of uh-SIS-ee**. Merriam-Webster also gives uh-SEE-see.

portrait.alt: A faded wall painting of a thin young friar in a grey hooded habit tied with a knotted cord, with dark eyes and a short beard, one hand on his chest. He has no halo, and the letters FR FRANCISCU stand beside his head

portrait.caption: Perhaps the oldest likeness of him, in the cave church of the Sacro Speco at Subiaco. It is said a monk painted it while he visited, maybe in 1218. It has no halo, no wounds, and calls him simply Brother Francis. Public domain.

west.text: His body carried into his new church at Assisi in 1230, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.
The marks of his wounds, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**. Since 1969 it is left to local calendars.
The **Episcopal Church**, in its *Lesser Feasts and Fasts* of 2022: the day he died.
**Catholic** memorial. Also a Lesser Festival in the **Church of England**, and a commemoration in the **ELCA**, as a renewer of the church.

feasts.note: Why 4 October? He died on the evening of the 3rd. His body was carried into Assisi on the 4th, and Celano dates his death to that day, a Sunday. When Gregory IX made him a saint, he ordered his feast kept “on the day of his death”. Rome's calendar of 1969 moved the feast of the wounds to local calendars, because it doubles the feast of 4 October. The Orthodox churches keep no day for him.

traits.title: joyful, on purpose
traits.text: He held that joy was the best guard against the devil: “The Devil most exults when he can filch from a servant of God his joy of spirit.” So, says Celano, “He strove therefore ever to be gladsome of heart.” When robbers stopped him in a wood, he was singing God's praises in French. He told them, “I am a herald of the great King.”

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 125; First Life, chapter 16

traits.title: courteous to everyone
traits.text: Once, still a merchant, he sent a beggar away rudely. He was so ashamed that he resolved to “never in future deny anything to any one asking him for the sake of God”. Celano adds that this was out of character, “for he was most courteous”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 17

traits.title: tender to every creature
traits.text: “Even towards little worms he glowed with exceeding love,” says Celano. He picked them off the path so no one would tread on them. When fish were caught, he would throw them back alive, “bidding them beware of being caught a second time”. In winter he had honey or the best wine set out for the bees. He called every creature brother or sister.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 61, 80 and 81

traits.title: hard on his own body
traits.text: He called his body Brother Ass. One winter night, fighting temptation, he threw himself into the snow and made seven heaps of it. He told his body, “this large one is thy wife”, and the rest were its children and servants, freezing and waiting to be clothed. At the end of his life he asked Brother Ass's pardon for treating it so harshly.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapters 116 and 117; Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

traits.title: no use for money
traits.text: His motto for the brothers was “Let dung and money be loved and valued alike”. A visitor once left coins at the church, and a brother touched them to put them on a window sill. Francis made him carry the money out in his mouth, and drop it on a heap of asses' dung.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 65

traits.title: small on purpose
traits.text: His *Rule* said of the brothers, “And be they lesser”. When it was read, he said, “I will that this brotherhood be called the Order of Lesser Brethren”, the Friars Minor. He never became a priest, and stayed a deacon all his life.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 38 and 86

said.lede: Thomas of Celano, a friar who knew him, wrote the first *Life* in 1228 and 1229, at the bidding of Pope Gregory IX. People have argued about him ever since.

quotes.q: He was stedfast in purpose, firm in virtue, persevering in grace, and in all things the same. He was swift to pardon and slow to be angry.
quotes.who: Thomas of Celano, who knew him

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 83, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell (1908)

quotes.q: The master of these Brothers is named Brother Francis; he is so lovable that he is venerated by everyone.
quotes.who: Jacques de Vitry, bishop of Acre, in a letter from the crusaders' camp in Egypt, 1220. In Paul Sabatier's French, put into English by Louise Houghton.

cite.text: Paul Sabatier, Life of St. Francis of Assisi (1894), tr. Louise Seymour Houghton

quotes.q: From out that slope, there where it breaketh most its steepness, rose upon the world a sun.
quotes.who: Dante, in *Paradise*, about 1320, on the hill of Assisi. Longfellow's translation.

cite.text: Dante, Paradiso, canto 11, tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867)

quotes.q: For he treated the whole mob of men as a mob of kings.
quotes.who: G. K. Chesterton, *St. Francis of Assisi*, 1923

cite.text: G. K. Chesterton, St. Francis of Assisi (1923), chapter 6

quotes.q: …a harmless enthusiast, pious and sincere, but hardly of sane mind…
quotes.who: The English historian Henry Hallam, early in the 1800s, as Thomas Okey quoted him in 1910, to disagree

cite.text: Thomas Okey, introduction to The Little Flowers (Everyman, 1910)

moments.title: The king of the feasts
moments.text: He worked in his father's cloth trade, but he was merrier and freer with money than his father. He went “round the city of Assisi day and night in company with his like”, and spent all he had on banquets. His parents said he lived like a prince's son, not theirs. When the neighbours talked, his mother answered: “What think ye of my son? He shall yet be the son of God by grace.”

cite.text: Legend of the Three Companions, chapter 1

moments.title: A year in chains
moments.text: Assisi went to war with Perugia, and Francis was taken prisoner. The other captives were gloomy, and he laughed at his chains. When they called him mad, he answered: “I shall yet be worshipped as a Saint all the world over.” There was a proud knight among them whom everyone shunned. Francis bore with him and got the others to make peace with him.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 4

moments.title: A dream of arms
moments.text: He set out to fight in Apulia, hungry for glory. Before he left, he dreamed his house was full of “saddles, shields, lances”, where there were usually bales of cloth. On the road, at Spoleto, a voice asked him in the night: “Which can do the better for thee, the lord, or the servant?” He said the lord. Then why leave the lord for the servant? He turned round and rode home.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 5; Legend of the Three Companions, chapter 2

moments.title: The leper
moments.text: Lepers had always disgusted him. Even when he saw their houses two miles off, he held his nose. Then one day, riding near Assisi, he met a leper. He got down from his horse and kissed him, and the leper, holding out his hand, “received money and a kiss with it”. Celano's second *Life* adds that when he looked back, “he could not see that leper at all”. Twenty years later he began his Testament with that day.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 17; Second Life, chapter 9

moments.title: “Repair My house”
moments.text: He went to pray in San Damiano, a crumbling church below the town. The painted crucifix spoke to him: “Francis, go repair My house, which as thou seest is wholly falling into ruin.” He took it as it sounded. He rode to Foligno, sold a load of scarlet cloth and the horse too, and offered the money to the priest. Then he set about rebuilding the church with his own hands.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 10; First Life, chapters 8, 9 and 18

moments.title: Naked before the bishop
moments.text: His father dragged him home and locked him up, then took him before Bishop Guido to get his money back. Francis gave the money back. Then, without a word, he took off all his clothes and handed them to his father. He “stripped himself stark naked before all the bystanders”. The bishop wrapped him in his own cloak.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 12 to 15; Second Life, chapter 12

moments.title: The Gospel of the road
moments.text: He was mending a third ruined church, St Mary of the Portiuncula, in the plain below Assisi. At Mass he heard the Gospel where Christ sends out His disciples with no gold, no bag, no staff and no shoes. He asked the priest to explain it, and cried: “This is what I wish, this is what I am seeking, this I long with all my inmost heart to do.” He took off his shoes, put down his staff and tied his tunic with a cord.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 21 and 22

moments.title: The Pope's dream
moments.text: Men of Assisi began to join him. With eleven brothers he went to Rome, to ask Pope Innocent III to approve a short rule taken from the Gospel. Celano's second *Life* says the Pope had lately dreamed that the Lateran basilica was falling, and that “a certain Religious, a man small and despised, was propping it on his own back”. Innocent approved the rule by word of mouth.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 32 and 33; Second Life, chapter 17

moments.title: Clare
moments.text: Clare was a young noblewoman of Assisi who had heard him preach. On the night after Palm Sunday she slipped out of her family's house by “a door much barred and obstructed with stones”, and came to the brothers at the Portiuncula. There her hair was cut off, and she gave her life to God. She soon settled at San Damiano, the church Francis had rebuilt, with the women who became the Poor Clares.

cite.text: The Life of St Clare, ascribed to Thomas of Celano, tr. Charlotte Balfour (1910); Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

moments.title: Across the lines
moments.text: During the Fifth Crusade he crossed from the Christian camp to the Muslim one. He was beaten by the soldiers, and brought before the Sultan of Egypt. The story is told below, in “Francis and the Sultan”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 57

moments.title: The *Rule* written twice
moments.text: His brothers now numbered thousands. His rule of 1221 was too long and loose to serve as a formal rule. He went up to Fonte Colombo, a hermitage near Rieti, and wrote a shorter one. He gave it to Brother Elias, his vicar, who not long after “declared he had lost it through negligence”. Francis went back and wrote it again, in twelve chapters. Pope Honorius III approved it on 29 November 1223, and the Friars Minor still profess it.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909); Paschal Robinson, The Writings of St Francis (1906)

moments.title: A manger in the woods
moments.text: Two weeks before Christmas he asked a friend at Greccio to prepare the feast: “I would make memorial of that Child Who was born in Bethlehem, and in some sort behold with bodily eyes His infant hardships.” The friend made ready a manger with hay, an ox and an ass. People came through the woods with torches. Mass was said over the manger, and Francis, a deacon, sang the Gospel. When he said “Bethlehem”, he said it “in the manner of a sheep bleating”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 84 to 86

moments.title: The Canticle that made peace
moments.text: Nearly blind and in pain, he stayed in a hut by San Damiano, where Clare and her sisters lived. There he made his *Canticle of the Sun*. Then the bishop and the mayor of Assisi fell out. He added a verse on those who forgive, and sent two brothers to sing it before them both. The mayor wept, and said that he would forgive even the murder of his own son: “if any one should have slain my blood-friend or my son I will forgive him”. The bishop answered: “My office bids me be humble, yet because I am naturally prompt to wrath, it behoves that thou shouldst pardon me.”

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909); The Mirror of Perfection, chapter 101, a compilation of about 1318, tr. Robert Steele

extras.title: Francis and the Sultan
extras.lede: In 1219 he walked out of the crusaders' camp and into the Sultan's. Three early writers tell it, each in their own way, and people still argue over what it meant.

items.title: The earliest witness
items.text: The Fifth Crusade was besieging Damietta, a port of Egypt. Jacques de Vitry, bishop of Acre, was in the Christian camp. He wrote home in 1220, soon after. His letter says the Sultan listened, and asked for a sign:
items.quote: For days together he announced the word of God to the Saracens, but with little success; then the sultan, King of Egypt, asked him in secret to entreat God to reveal to him, by some miracle, which is the best religion.

cite.text: Jacques de Vitry, letter of 1220, in Paul Sabatier, Life of St. Francis of Assisi (1894), tr. Louise Seymour Houghton

items.title: Celano, ten years on
items.text: In Celano's first *Life*, the Sultan's soldiers seize him, insult him and beat him. The Sultan himself receives him with honour and offers him rich gifts. Francis refuses them all, and the Sultan is amazed:
items.quote: He was deeply stirred by his words and heard him very willingly.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 57

items.title: The fire, forty years later
items.text: Bonaventure's *Life*, written about 1260, adds a challenge. Francis offers to walk into a great fire with the Sultan's priests, or alone, if the Sultan and his people will believe. The Sultan says no. His priests would not do it, he answers, and he fears his people would revolt. Paul Sabatier doubted the story in 1894: “We know how little such an appeal to signs is characteristic of St. Francis.” In Bonaventure the Sultan answers:
items.quote: I do not believe that any of my priests would be ready to expose himself unto the fire in defence of his faith, or to undergo any sort of torture.

cite.text: Bonaventure, Life of St Francis, chapter 9, tr. E. Gurney Salter; Sabatier (1894)

items.title: Two readings
items.text: The early *Lives* say plainly why he went. Celano speaks of “the lofty purpose to attain martyrdom”. Bonaventure says he went “that by the shedding of his blood the Faith of the Trinity might be spread abroad”. He came back alive, and the Sultan stayed a Muslim. His own *Rule* of 1221 gives brothers going among Muslims two ways. “One way is not to make disputes or contentions”, living among them and owning they are Christians. The second is open preaching: “The other way is that when they see it is pleasing to God, they announce the Word of God.” Some read him as a missionary who meant to convert the Sultan or die. Others see a bridge between two faiths. G. K. Chesterton, in 1923, called it a great effort that
items.quote: broke off short like the beginnings of a great bridge that might have united East and West, and remains one of the great might-have-beens of history

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 56; Bonaventure, chapter 9; Rule of 1221, chapter 16; Chesterton, St. Francis of Assisi (1923)

miracles.lede: Celano wrote his first *Life* at the Pope's bidding, just after the canonisation and less than three years after the death. It ends with a long list of healings at the tomb. At the start he says where his stories come from:

pledge.q: …those things that I have heard from blessed Francis' own mouth or have understood from faithful and approved witnesses…

cite.text: Celano, First Life, preface

items.title: The seraph
items.text: Two years before he died, he was keeping a long fast on the mountain of La Verna. In a vision he saw a man like a seraph, with six wings, fixed to a cross. He was glad at its kind look and afraid of its suffering, and could not tell what it meant. Then his own body began to change.
items.quote: marks of nails began to appear in his hands and feet, such as he had seen a little while before in the Man crucified Who had stood over him
items.witness: Brother Leo was with him. On the sheet Francis wrote for him there, Leo noted that it was made “after the vision and speech of the Seraph and the impression of the Stigmata of Christ in his body”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 94; Brother Leo's note, in Robinson (1906)

items.title: Hidden
items.text: His hands and feet bore what looked like nails made of his own flesh, with round heads on one side and bent points on the other. His right side had a wound that often bled on his tunic. He hid them from nearly everyone. Once Brother Rufino, reaching into his tunic to scratch an itch for him, touched the wound in his side. Francis pushed his hand away and asked the Lord to forgive him.
items.quote: he concealed the stigmata most diligently from strangers
items.witness: Brother Elias saw the side wound while he lived, and Rufino, says Celano, “touched it with his own hands”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 95

items.title: Seen by all
items.text: When he died, the brothers kissed his hands and feet, and the people of Assisi crowded in to see. Celano says they saw in his flesh
items.quote: not the prints of the nails but the nails themselves formed out of his flesh and retaining the blackness of iron
items.witness: Brother Elias, his vicar, wrote to the whole Order the next day: “For a long time before his death our Brother and Father appeared as crucified, having in his body five wounds which are truly the stigmata of Christ.”

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 112 and 113; Elias's letter of 1226, in Sabatier (1894)

note.text: Nine years after his death, Bonaventura Berlinghieri painted him for the church at Pescia with the wounds in his hands and feet. The panel is dated 1235, and it is still at Pescia.

cite.text: Sabatier (1894), Critical study of the stigmata; the panel at Pescia

more.title: The sermon to the birds
more.text: Near Bevagna he saw a great gathering of birds: doves, rooks and others. He left his companions on the road and ran to them, and they did not fly away. So he preached to them. The birds stretched their necks, spread their wings and gazed at him, as he and his brothers used to tell it. After that he blamed himself for never having preached to birds before.
more.quote: My brother birds, much ought ye to praise your Creator, and ever to love Him Who has given you feathers for clothing, wings for flight, and all that ye had need of.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 58

more.title: The swallows at Alviano
more.text: He stood up to preach at the fortress of Alviano, but the swallows nesting there chattered so loudly that no one could hear. He spoke to them, and they were silent until the sermon was over. The people said: “Truly this man is a Saint, and a friend of the Most High”.
more.quote: My sisters, the swallows, it is now time for me to speak too, because you have been saying enough all this time.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 59

more.title: Brother Fire
more.text: His eyes were failing, and a surgeon came to burn his temple with a red-hot iron, from the ear to the eyebrow. The brothers fled. Francis spoke to the fire as his brother, and asked it to be gentle. The iron went in hissing. When the brothers came back, he told them he had felt nothing. The surgeon said: “I tell you, brethren, I have seen wondrous things to-day”.
more.quote: I tell you of a truth I felt no heat of fire nor any pain in my flesh.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 166

more.title: The wolves of Greccio
more.text: The people of Greccio were plagued by wolves and by hail. He preached to them and promised them relief if they turned back to God. From that hour, says Celano,
more.quote: nor did wolves nor hail cause any further mischief

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 35

more.title: A later legend: the wolf of Gubbio
more.text: His most famous animal story is not in Celano or Bonaventure. It is in the *Little Flowers*, an Italian book made from a Latin collection compiled some time after 1322, a century after his death. A wolf is eating the people of Gubbio. Francis goes out alone, makes the sign of the cross, and the wolf lies down at his feet. He makes a peace: the town will feed the wolf, and the wolf will harm no one. The wolf lays its paw in his hand.
more.quote: Friar wolf, I desire that thou pledge thy faith to me to keep this promise, that I may have full trust in thee.

cite.text: The Little Flowers, chapter 21, tr. Thomas Okey (1910)

doubt.title: Doubted, and defended
doubt.text: The wounds were doubted early. In 1237 Pope Gregory IX wrote to all the faithful to affirm them, and rebuked a bishop of Olmütz, in Moravia, and the Dominicans for calling them in question. Later writers said Brother Elias had made them, in a pious fraud. Paul Sabatier, a French Protestant historian, set that aside: Elias's opponents in the Order, Leo, Angelo and Rufino, would have had to be in on it. He believed the wounds were real, but not a miracle: “They may have been a unique fact without being more miraculous than other phenomena.” On the Orthodox side, the Russian theologian Alexei Osipov writes that such wounds are known to psychiatry and have nothing supernatural in them. The Orthodox Church in America says that stigmata “are foreign to the Orthodox experience”. Even Celano has been doubted. His translator Howell reports the Italian scholar Tamassia's charge that his *Lives* were stitched together from older books, among them Gregory the Great and Sulpicius, the biographer of Martin of Tours. Howell himself found the case unproven.

cites.text: Paul Sabatier, Life of St. Francis of Assisi (1894), Critical study of the stigmata
A. I. Osipov, Tell Me Who Your Saints Are, in English on John Sanidopoulos's site
A. G. Ferrers Howell, introduction to The Lives of S. Francis (1908)

words.note: Unlike most early saints, Francis wrote. His two Rules, his Testament, letters, prayers and the *Canticle of the Sun* survive. His writings are given here in Paschal Robinson's translation of 1906, and his spoken words as Thomas of Celano recorded them, in A. G. Ferrers Howell's translation of 1908.

feature.q: When I was in sin it seemed to me very bitter to see lepers, and the Lord Himself led me amongst them and I showed mercy to them. And when I left them, that which had seemed to me bitter was changed for me into sweetness of body and soul.
feature.ctx: The first lines of the Testament he left his brothers as he was dying. It opens with the leper.

cite.text: Testament of St Francis, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)

quotes.q: Henceforth I may freely say ‘Our Father Who art in heaven,’ not any more ‘father Pietro di Bernardone,’ to whom lo! I not only restore the money but give up all my clothes.
quotes.who: Before the bishop of Assisi, as he gave his father back even his clothes.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 12

quotes.q: The Lord revealed to me this salutation, that we should say: “The Lord give thee peace.”

cite.text: Testament of St Francis, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)

quotes.q: What a man is in the sight of God, so much he is, and no more.
quotes.who: From his Admonitions. *The Imitation of Christ* repeats it two centuries later.

cite.text: Admonitions, 20, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)

quotes.q: I need no more, my son: I know Christ, the poor man crucified.
quotes.who: When he was ill, and a brother offered to read him the Prophets for comfort.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 105

quotes.q: I say to thee: Yes, my son, and as a mother.
quotes.who: To Brother Leo, who was troubled with doubts, in a letter that survives in his own hand at Spoleto. It ends: “Leo, to come to me, come!”

cite.text: Letter to Brother Leo, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)

myths.claim: He said, “Preach the Gospel at all times. Use words if necessary.”
myths.truth: No such line is in his writings or in any early *Life*. The nearest is his *Rule* of 1221, on preachers: “Nevertheless, let all the brothers preach by their works.” But he preached with words all his life, and his *Rule* of 1223 tells his preachers to speak “with brevity of speech because the Lord made His word short upon earth”.

cite.text: Rule of 1221, chapter 17; Rule of 1223, chapter 9; The Gospel Coalition, FactChecker

myths.claim: He wrote the Peace Prayer, “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.”
myths.truth: It first appeared in December 1912, in French and unsigned, in a small Paris magazine called *La Clochette*: “Seigneur, faites de moi un instrument de votre paix.” About 1920 it was printed on the back of a picture of St Francis, without his name. It was first called his in 1927, and the first known English version is from 1936. Its shape does echo his real Admonitions: “Where there is poverty and joy there is neither cupidity nor avarice.”

cite.text: Christian Renoux, The Origin of the Peace Prayer of St. Francis, Franciscan Archive; Admonitions, 27

myths.claim: He tamed the wolf of Gubbio.
myths.truth: The story is first told in the Latin collection behind the *Little Flowers*, compiled some time after 1322. Celano, writing about twenty years after his death, tells only of wolves that stopped troubling Greccio after he preached. Thomas Okey, who translated the *Little Flowers* in 1910, suggested that a brigand nicknamed Brother Wolf, or a cruel lord, “may easily have been developed into the fierce wolf of Gubbio”.

cite.text: Thomas Okey, introduction to The Little Flowers (1910); Celano, Second Life, chapter 35

myths.claim: He walked through fire to convert the Sultan.
myths.truth: In Bonaventure's *Life* of about 1260 he offers to, and the Sultan declines. Jacques de Vitry and Celano, the earliest writers, tell no such offer. The Sultan did not become a Christian.

cite.text: Bonaventure, chapter 9; Sabatier (1894)

myths.truth: He was a deacon. At Greccio, Celano notes that he sang the Gospel “for he was a Levite”, the old word for a deacon. The Episcopal Church's book of saints says “he resisted all efforts to persuade him to become a priest”.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 86; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 3 October

myths.claim: He made the first nativity set, with Mary, Joseph and the Baby.
myths.truth: Celano's account of Greccio has a manger with hay, an ox and an ass, and Mass said over the manger. It mentions no figures of Mary, Joseph or the Child. One man there saw, in a vision, a child lying in the manger.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 84 to 86

myths.claim: He was born in a stable, like Christ.
myths.truth: A legend of the 1400s. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says it came from “the desire of certain writers to make his life resemble that of Christ”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909), St. Francis of Assisi

circle.name: Clare of Assisi
circle.text: A young noblewoman of Assisi who ran from home to follow him in 1212. She led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano for about forty years. His funeral procession stopped there so that she could see him.

cite.text: The Life of St Clare (1910); Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

circle.name: Pietro di Bernardone
circle.text: His father, a rich cloth merchant. He fought his son's new life with curses and chains, and took him before the bishop for his money.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 10 to 15; Second Life, chapter 12

circle.name: Pica
circle.text: His mother. In his wild youth she told the neighbours that he would yet be a son of God.

cite.text: Legend of the Three Companions, chapter 1

circle.name: Guido, bishop of Assisi
circle.text: He wrapped Francis in his own cloak when he stripped, and stood by him in Rome in 1209.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapters 15 and 32

circle.name: Bernard of Quintavalle
circle.text: His first companion. Francis blessed him by name as he was dying.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

circle.name: Brother Leo
circle.text: His closest friend among the brothers, and with him on La Verna. He kept the sheet Francis wrote for him, and noted on it when and why it was written.

cite.text: Paschal Robinson, The Writings of St Francis (1906)

circle.name: Brother Elias
circle.text: His vicar in the last years. He announced the wounds to the Order, and built the great church at Assisi. He later fell out with the brothers and with Pope Gregory IX, who excommunicated him.

cite.text: Sabatier (1894); Howell's index to Celano (1908)

circle.name: Pope Innocent III
circle.text: He approved the first rule by word of mouth, after dreaming that a small, despised man held up the Lateran.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapter 17

circle.name: Pope Gregory IX
circle.text: As Cardinal Hugolino he protected the brothers. As Pope he made Francis a saint in 1228, and told Celano to write his *Life*.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, preface and chapters 119 to 126

circle.name: Al-Malik al-Kamil
circle.text: The Sultan of Egypt, who received him in his camp at Damietta in 1219.

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 57; Jacques de Vitry (1220)

circle.name: Jacoba of Settesoli
circle.text: A Roman noblewoman he called “Brother Jacoba”. She came to his deathbed, and he let her in, though women were not allowed in the friary.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

circle.name: Thomas of Celano
circle.text: A friar who joined him about 1215. He wrote the first *Life* in 1228 and 1229, and a second between 1244 and 1247, from the memories of his companions.

cite.text: A. G. Ferrers Howell, introduction to The Lives of S. Francis (1908)

death.big: He died at the Portiuncula, below Assisi, on the evening of 3 October 1226. He was 44.
paras: For two years he had been ill: his eyes, his whole body, the wounds. He asked to be carried down to the Portiuncula, where his Order began. He blessed the brothers one by one, and had bread broken and shared among them, as at the Last Supper.

At the end he asked to be laid naked on the bare ground, and covered the wound in his side with his hand. The Passion from John's Gospel was read to him. He began Psalm 142, “I cried unto the Lord with my voice”, and died at its last verse: “Bring my soul out of prison”.

The next day his body was carried up into Assisi. The procession stopped at San Damiano, so that Clare and her sisters could see him. In 1230 he was moved to the great church built in his honour, and hidden under the altar so deep that no one could find him until 1818.

later.title: The larks
later.text: Bonaventure, writing about 1260, adds that at the hour he died the larks, “birds that love the light, and dread the shades of twilight”, came to the roof in great numbers as night fell, and wheeled over it singing.

cite.text: Bonaventure, Life of St Francis, chapter 14, tr. E. Gurney Salter

items.k: To the brothers, from the bare ground
items.q: I have done my duty, may Christ teach you yours.

items.ctx: He had added a verse to his Canticle for “our sister, the bodily death”.

cite.text: Celano, Second Life, chapters 214 and 217

saint.big: Yes, for Catholics and Anglicans, and Lutherans remember him. The Orthodox churches do not count him among their saints.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England
ELCA, 4 October; not in the Missouri Synod's calendar
He lived after the split of 1054

paras: He was made a saint quickly. Pope Gregory IX, who had known him as a friend, canonised him at Assisi on 16 July 1228, less than two years after he died. The cardinals said that miracles were hardly needed:

The Orthodox churches keep no day for him. He lived in the West after the break between the churches in 1054, and it was Rome that declared him a saint. The Orthodox Church in America has no official position on stigmata, and some Orthodox writers treat his visions as a spiritual danger. The old *Roman Martyrology* gives him this line:

quotes.q: No need for miracles to attest the most holy man's most holy life, which we have seen with our eyes, handled with our hands and proved under the teaching of truth.
quotes.who: The cardinals, meeting at Perugia to decide his canonisation

cite.text: Celano, First Life, chapter 124

quotes.q: At Assisi, in Umbria, the birthday of St. Francis, confessor, founder of the Order of Minorites, whose life, filled with holy deeds and miracles, was written by St. Bonaventure.
quotes.who: The *Roman Martyrology*, 1916 edition, for 4 October. A saint's “birthday” is the day he died.

cite.text: The Roman Martyrology (1916)

prayer.intro: The opening of the *Canticle of the Sun*, which he made at San Damiano in 1225, in the Umbrian speech of his day. Paschal Robinson kept his translation plain and close to the original. Pope Francis took the title of his 2015 letter on care for our common home from its refrain, “Laudato si’, mi’ Signore”, and William Draper's hymn *All Creatures of Our God and King* is an English version of it.
prayer.q: Most high, omnipotent, good Lord, praise, glory and honor and benediction all, are Thine. To Thee alone do they belong, most High, and there is no man fit to mention Thee. Praise be to Thee, my Lord, with all Thy creatures, especially to my worshipful brother sun, the which lights up the day, and through him dost Thou brightness give; and beautiful is he and radiant with splendor great; of Thee, most High, signification gives. Praised be my Lord, for sister moon and for the stars, in heaven Thou hast formed them clear and precious and fair.

cite.text: The Canticle of the Sun, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)
